fetched_contents.text: Complications of corneal collagen cross-linking Abstract Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) is an effective treatment for arresting progression in patients with keratoconus. CXL was approved by United States Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of progressive keratoconus in 2016. It is a relatively safe procedure with a low complication rate. As this approach becomes more popular, it is paramount to be familiar with the potential complications associated with the procedure and its management. This article aims to report and review the complications of CXL for the treatment of keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia. Keywords: Complications, corneal collagen cross-linking, CXL, epi-on CXL, keratoconus, post-LASIK ectasia, transepithelial cross-linking ---------------------------------------- Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) is a minimally invasive procedure for keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia, to arrest progression of keratectasia.[1] Induction of cross-links in corneal stroma result in stiffening and strengthening of ectatic cornea. It has also been used for the management of other conditions such as bullous keratopathy, infective and ulcerative keratitis.[2] CXL involves the application of commercially manufactured ophthalmic riboflavin (vitamin B2) solution and UVA to the corneal stroma. The combination of riboflavin and UV-A induces the production of free oxygen radicals, which allows for the formation of new covalent bonds in stromal collagen improving the biomechanical and biochemical properties of the cornea, especially essential in management of keratoconus and postlasik ectasia.[3] Clinical results of CXL in keratectasia include arresting progression of the condition, vision preservation, possible improvement of topographic shape, better fit of contact lenses, and preventing the future need for keratoplasty.[4,5,6] The antimicrobial activity of riboflavin and UVA and corneal resistance to CXL have been described,[7,8] and these characteristics make CXL treatment a good option for managing infective keratitis and infectious ulcers, as CXL can improve the corneal ability to resist proteolytic enzymes secreted by infective microorganisms. This concept of treating corneal ectatic disorder with riboflavin/ultraviolet A (UVA) corneal cross-linking (CXL) was postulated by Spoerl and colleagues at the University of Dresden.[3,4] It was first done in porcine eyes which showed up to 70% increase in corneal rigidity compared to controls[3] and then was repeated in rabbit[9] and human cadaver eyes.[9,10] Based on these studies, the safety of cross-linking was ascertained and was also found to be related to corneal thickness to avoid damage to the corneal endothelium and other ocular structures.[11] The first report of the use of CXL in keratoconus was published in 2003.[4] Wollensak et al.[4] crosslinked 23 eyes with progressive keratoconus, resulting in halting progression in all eyes and corneal flattening in up to 70%. Further clinical studies showed similar promising results in patients with ectasia after refractive surgery.[12] The estimated incidence of keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia are 0.001–0.03[13] and 0.04–0.6%,[14] respectively. Several techniques have been developed in the past decade to increase the efficacy of CXL. The conventional Dresden protocol (C-CXL), accelerated corneal crosslinking (A-CXL), transepithelial (T-CXL) techniques using chemical enhancers, and iontophoresis crosslinking techniques (I-CXL) are some of the commonly used and currently investigated procedures in clinical practice. CXL has proved to be an effective treatment for most cases. However, besides the transient reversible side effects, some cases with complications such as corneal haze and scarring, reduced uncorrected and best spectacle-corrected visual acuity, infectious and noninfectious keratitis, stromal melting, and treatment failure with the progression of ectasia have been reported.[15] This article aims to report and review the complications of CXL, otherwise a safe procedure, for the treatment of keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia. Methods of Literature Search A search of the PubMed database was conducted for “complications of CXL” and each of the following keywords: CXL, corneal cross linking, collagen cross linking, keratoconus, ectasia after LASIK, complications and cross-linking, progression, and trans-epithelial CXL. We limited our search to articles published from 1998 to present day that were written in English or the abstracts were in English. The search was conducted in August 2020. All abstracts were screened, and relevant articles were included in this review. Complications Removal of corneal epithelium is performed conventionally to facilitate penetration of riboflavin into the corneal stroma.[16] The classic Dresden protocol, introduced by Wollensask et al.[4] in 2003, involves the removal of the corneal epithelium followed by application of riboflavin solution (0.1% riboflavin in 20% dextran solution) to the deepithelialized cornea for 30 min, then the cornea is irradiated with UVA (wavelength, 370 nm and power, 3 mW/cm2) for another 30 min. The riboflavin solution is applied every 3–5 min during the irradiation process. This corresponds to a total energy administration of 5.4 J/cm2, which was found to be efficacious for tissue stiffening.[4,17] Epithelial removal can lead to potential complications. Pain, epithelial defects, infectious and non-infectious keratitis, corneal opacity, reduced visual acuity, and blurred vision were the most common reported adverse events in various clinical trials.[15,18,19,20] Pain Removal of epithelium causes significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days. Pain is a common complaint with crosslinking. fetched_contents.text: Transepithelial corneal cross-linking: a review Abstract Purpose This review aims to summarize the current understanding of transepithelial corneal cross-linking (TE-CXL) for treating keratoconus (KC). It focuses on how TE-CXL compares with the standard epithelium-off cross-linking (S-CXL) and discusses recent improvements intended to make it more effective. Methods Relevant studies were reviewed from PubMed and Google Scholar. The review focused on research about new riboflavin solutions, delivery techniques, ultraviolet-A (UV-A) light settings, oxygen supply methods, and recent new technologies designed to improve the results of TE-CXL. Results TE-CXL preserves the corneal epithelium, providing better patient comfort and fewer postoperative complications. However, its corneal stiffening effect is generally lower than S-CXL due to limited riboflavin penetration and UV photoactivation. Recent approaches, including chemical enhancers, iontophoresis-assisted delivery, optimized UV-A protocols, nanotechnology-based or ultrasound-assisted methods have demonstrated potential to improve biomechanical strengthening. In addition, theranostic-guided TE-CXL, which provides real-time monitoring of stromal riboflavin concentration and adaptive UV-A dosing, represents a promising advancement. Nevertheless, differences in treatment protocols and in oxygen and luminance parameters still lead to variability in clinical outcomes. Conclusions TE-CXL is a promising and less invasive treatment for KC, offering better comfort and faster recovery. However, its long-term stability and biomechanical effect remain inferior to S-CXL. Future progress will depend on optimizing riboflavin and oxygen delivery, refining UV-A irradiation protocols, and validating newer technologies such as theranostic-guided CXL through large-scale clinical studies. Keywords: Keratoconus, Crosslinking, Transepithelial corneal cross-linking, Riboflavin penetration, Corneal epithelium Introduction Keratoconus (KC) is a progressive corneal ectatic disorder characterized by bilateral thinning of the central, paracentral, or peripheral corneal tissue [1]. Although KC was traditionally considered a non-inflammatory condition, increasing evidence indicates that inflammatory and oxidative-stress–related pathways may contribute to its onset and progression [2]. This thinning leads to irregular astigmatism, progressive myopia, and an increase in higher-order aberrations (HOAs), which can ultimately result in significant vision loss [3, 4]. KC usually develops around puberty, but it is most commonly diagnosed in the second and third decades of life. The disease progressively worsens into the fourth decade, after which the progression usually stops, and the condition stabilizes [5]. Epidemiological studies estimate the prevalence of KC to range from 0.2 to 4,790 per 100,000 individuals, particularly in Asian populations [6, 7]. Recent studies using advanced imaging suggest KC prevalence is higher than previously reported, with significant variability across populations [8, 9]. Population-based studies using Scheimpflug imaging and Placido-disk topography report higher prevalence rates and can even detect earlier stages of keratoconus, indicating that earlier estimates substantially underestimated the true disease burden [10, 11]. Corneal cross-linking (CXL) is a treatment developed to address the progression of the KC by re-strengthening the corneal collagen matrix, ultimately reducing or delaying the need for corneal transplantation. This treatment uses ultraviolet-A light and riboflavin, inducing the production of reactive oxygen species, which facilitate the formation of additional covalent bonds between collagen molecules [12]. This CXL process enhances the rigidity and stability of the corneal structure. The standard epithelium-off cross-linking (S-CXL) approach, commonly referred to as the Dresden protocol, removes the central corneal epithelium to facilitate adequate diffusion of riboflavin and oxygen into the stroma [13–16]. Although S-CXL remains the clinical standard due to its well-established efficacy in halting KC progression, epithelial removal is associated with postoperative pain, delayed epithelial healing, and a higher risk of infection and stromal haze, both of which are relatively uncommon complications. [17–25]. Therefore, although S-CXL is the most widely performed and accepted standard worldwide, the development of transepithelial CXL (TE-CXL) has generated ongoing debate regarding its efficacy and long-term outcomes. With the introduction of TE-CXL, the epithelium remains intact during the CXL procedure, offering advantages such as faster healing, reduced discomfort, quicker visual recovery, and a lower risk of corneal infection [26]. Despite these potential benefits, TE-CXL presents with several technical challenges, including limited riboflavin penetration, reduced UV penetration, and restricted oxygen diffusion due to the intact epithelial barrier, raising concerns about achieving adequate CXL treatment depth [27, 28]. Several meta-analyses have explored the efficacy of TE-CXL compared to S-CXL. Most systematic reviews indicate that TE-CXL is generally less effective than S-CXL in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement [29–31]. A small numbers of studies have reported comparable outcomes between S-CXL and TE-CXL, particularly with improvements in corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) [32–34]. However, the preponderance of evidence favors S-CXL, which remains the reference standard pending further high-quality comparative trials. These conflicting findings highlight the need for further high-quality randomized controlled trials to clarify the comparative efficacy of TE-CXL and S-CXL. Despite this, TE-CXL techniques are particularly appealing because they avoid epithelial removal, reducing associated risks and enabling faster postoperative recovery. Mini-report on complications for epithelium-off cross-linking

Epithelium-off corneal cross-linking is associated with the most commonly reported adverse events in the evidence, including pain, epithelial defects, infectious and non-infectious keratitis, corneal opacity, reduced visual acuity, and blurred vision [N1-F1]. The review explicitly lists these as the most common reported adverse events in various clinical trials [N1-F1]. Serious complications are also reported, such as corneal haze and scarring, reduced uncorrected and best spectacle-corrected visual acuity, infectious and noninfectious keratitis, stromal melting, and treatment failure with progression of ectasia [N1-F1].

The pain profile is prominent: epithelium removal causes significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days, and pain is a common complaint with cross-linking [N1-F1]. Epithelial healing is another key issue: delayed epithelial healing, sterile infiltrates, epithelial defects, pain, or infiltrates are described as common complications following the procedure [N1-R3]. The review also notes that removal of epithelium can lead to potential complications, including pain, epithelial defects, infectious and non-infectious keratitis, corneal opacity, reduced visual acuity, and blurred vision [N1-F1].

Haze is a notable outcome. The review states that haze and scarring are reported complications, and it also notes that corneal haze is one of the most noticed adverse events associated with cross-linking [N2-R2]. Infection risk is emphasized by the post-operative management source, which highlights preventing infection as a key management goal [N4-R5]. Epithelial healing is directly tied to complication risk: patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for additional complications, including infection and corneal melting [N2-R1].

In terms of patient and disease factors that increase complication risk, the evidence is mixed but suggestive. Persistent epithelial defects are a clear risk factor for infection and melting [N2-R1]. The review also notes that removal of epithelium can lead to complications, which implies that preoperative epithelial status may matter [N1-F1]. While the provided evidence does not offer a complete list of risk factors, the strongest recurrent themes are epithelial integrity, infection prevention, and the possibility of delayed healing [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-R5].

Mini-report on complications for tranepithelial cross-linking

Tranepithelial cross-linking is also associated with complications, but the evidence indicates a different complication profile than epithelium-off CXL. The review notes that corneal haze and scarring are reported complications of CXL generally [N1-F1], and the post-operative management source emphasizes hastening re-epithelialization, preventing infection, and reducing pain [N4-R5]. A separate source explicitly states that patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting [N2-R1], which is relevant to tranepithelial cases because the epithelium remains intact during the procedure.

The most common adverse events are pain, epithelial defects, infectious and non-infectious keratitis, corneal opacity, reduced visual acuity, and blurred vision [N1-F1]. Tranepithelial CXL is not exempt from these; the evidence also reports infectious crystalline keratopathy after cross-linking as a case example, showing that infection-related complications can occur even with transepithelial approaches [N2-R4]. Haze is again a recurring issue: the review identifies haze and scarring as reported complications, while a separate source states that cross-linking-associated corneal haze is one of the most noticed adverse events [N2-R2].

Epithelial healing differs from epithelium-off CXL in that tranepithelial CXL avoids the need for epithelial removal, which may reduce postoperative pain and epithelial defects. However, the evidence suggests that tranepithelial CXL may still result in epithelial defects, infection, and haze [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The evidence also indicates that persistent epithelial defects can lead to infection and melting [N2-R1], so even though tranepithelial CXL may preserve the epithelium, complications can still arise if epithelial integrity is compromised during or after the procedure.

Patient and disease factors increasing complication risk include persistent epithelial defects and infection risk. The evidence directly states that patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting [N2-R1]. The review also notes that corneal haze and scarring are reported complications, and post-operative management emphasizes infection prevention [N1-F1][N4-R5]. While the evidence does not provide a full list of risk factors, the strongest signals are epithelial defect persistence and infection susceptibility [N2-R1][N1-F1].

Mini-report on clinical benefits and comparative efficacy

The evidence suggests that epithelium-off and tranepithelial cross-linking are both used in keratoconus and corneal ectasia, and that the choice between them is partly determined by complication risk and recovery profile rather than a clear overall superiority in stiffness alone [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. One study found that both techniques were effective at improving visual acuity and keratometry outcomes, but the primary outcomes showed no significant difference [N3-R1]. Another source says that tranepithelial CXL may result in little to no difference in CDVA at 12 months or beyond, and four studies reported no adverse events or minimal complications [N3-R5]. This implies that the two methods may be similarly effective in some key outcomes, but tranepithelial CXL may offer a less painful or faster recovery profile.

Best-corrected visual acuity is a major outcome. The evidence repeatedly notes that CXL is used to improve best-corrected visual acuity and stabilize keratoconus or ectasia [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The review also states that clinical results include arresting progression, vision preservation, possible improvement of topographic shape, better fit of contact lenses, and preventing the need for keratoplasty [N1-F1]. For tranepithelial CXL, the evidence indicates that outcomes such as CDVA can be maintained with little or no difference at 12 months or beyond [N3-R5]. In terms of functional improvement, the evidence points to improved keratometry, better contact lens fit, and preservation of vision [N1-F1].

Long-term efficacy and retreatment rates are less clearly resolved in the provided evidence, but some signals emerge. The review reports that treatment failure with progression of ectasia has been noted [N1-F1], and the comparative study notes that outcomes were sustained in some follow-ups [N3-R3]. The evidence also suggests that both methods can improve corneal rigidity and stiffness, but the comparative evidence is not definitive on whether one method is clearly superior to the other in that respect [N1-F1][N3-R1]. The review emphasizes that CXL is a relatively safe procedure with a low complication rate, but also notes that some cases have complications such as haze, scarring, reduced visual acuity, and treatment failure [N1-F1]. The comparative study suggests that tranepithelial CXL may be associated with fewer complications or less pain, but the evidence does not show a large difference in CDVA or keratometry outcomes [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a trade-off between complication risk and recovery time: epithelium-off CXL tends to be more painful and has a higher risk of epithelial defects, infection, haze, and melting, while tranepithelial CXL may be less painful and have better epithelial healing but still carries infection and haze risks [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-R5][N3-R5]. The comparative efficacy evidence does not support a clear winner on stiffness alone, and visual outcomes appear to be similarly improved in both methods in some studies [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Mini-report on clinical context and practical recommendations

Indications are best suited to each method based on the balance of efficacy, comfort, and complication risk. Epithelium-off cross-linking remains the standard of care for progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia because it provides the strongest established biomechanical effect and is the reference standard for comparative trials [N5-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The review explicitly states that S-CXL is the most widely performed and accepted standard worldwide and that its efficacy in halting KC progression is well established [N5-F2]. Tranepithelial cross-linking is best suited when faster healing, reduced discomfort, and lower infection risk are priorities, especially in patients who may benefit from less invasive treatment [N5-F2]. The review emphasizes that TE-CXL preserves the corneal epithelium, providing better patient comfort and fewer postoperative complications, but its corneal stiffening effect is generally lower than S-CXL [N5-F2].

Guideline or expert consensus recommendations are strongly suggestive but not fully explicit in the provided evidence. The review states that TE-CXL is a promising and less invasive treatment for keratoconus, offering better comfort and faster recovery, but its long-term stability and biomechanical effect remain inferior to S-CXL [N5-F2]. It also notes that most systematic reviews indicate TE-CXL is generally less effective than S-CXL in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2]. The evidence further indicates that epithelium-off CXL is associated with postoperative pain, delayed epithelial healing, and a higher risk of infection and stromal haze, both relatively uncommon complications [N5-F2]. Taken together, the consensus direction is that S-CXL is preferred for definitive stabilization and biomechanical strengthening, while TE-CXL is preferred for patients where comfort and recovery time are more important [N5-F2][N1-F1].

Trade-offs between complications, recovery time, and efficacy are central. Epithelium-off CXL is associated with more pain, higher risk of epithelial defects, infection, haze, and delayed healing, but it is generally more effective at improving corneal stiffness and biomechanical reinforcement [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Tranepithelial CXL has the advantages of better comfort, faster healing, quicker visual recovery, and lower infection risk, but it is associated with less corneal stiffening and potentially less durable biomechanical effect [N5-F2]. The comparative efficacy evidence is mixed: some studies suggest that outcomes such as CDVA can be maintained with little or no difference at 12 months or beyond, but the overall evidence favors S-CXL as the reference standard [N5-F2][N3-R5]. In practice, patients with progressive disease or those at higher risk of complications may be better suited to S-CXL, while patients with mild disease or those who prioritize comfort may be better suited to TE-CXL [N5-F2][N1-F1].

Practical recommendations should therefore depend on the clinical situation. For progressive keratoconus or corneal ectasia, the evidence supports using epithelium-off CXL as the standard treatment if the goal is maximum biomechanical reinforcement and stabilization [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]. For patients who can tolerate less invasive treatment and where faster recovery is important, tranepithelial CXL may be appropriate, particularly when combined with adjunctive techniques to improve riboflavin penetration and UV-A delivery [N5-F2]. The review also emphasizes that differences in treatment protocols and in oxygen and luminance parameters still lead to variability in clinical outcomes, so the choice should be guided by patient preference, disease severity, and the availability of optimized TE-CXL protocols [N5-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports a preference for epithelium-off CXL where efficacy is the priority and for tranepithelial CXL where comfort and recovery time are more important [N5-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1].

## Integrated final answer: main complications and clinical benefits of epithelium-off versus tranepithelial cross-linking

Epithelium-off and tranepithelial corneal cross-linking are both used in keratoconus and corneal ectasia, but they differ substantially in complication risk, recovery profile, and the balance of efficacy and patient comfort. The evidence suggests that epithelium-off cross-linking is generally the more established standard, while tranepithelial cross-linking is less invasive but not without its own complications [N5-F2][N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

---

## 1) Main complications

### Epithelium-off cross-linking

The most commonly reported adverse events in the evidence include **pain**, **epithelial defects**, **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, **corneal opacity**, **reduced visual acuity**, and **blurred vision** [N1-F1]. A more specific review also lists **corneal haze and scarring**, **reduced uncorrected and best spectacle-corrected visual acuity**, **infectious and noninfectious keratitis**, **stromal melting**, and **treatment failure with progression of ectasia** as reported complications [N1-F1]. The review also notes that removal of epithelium can lead to complications including **pain**, **epithelial defects**, **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, **corneal opacity**, **reduced visual acuity**, and **blurred vision** [N1-F1].

Epithelial healing is a key issue: **delayed epithelial healing**, **sterile infiltrates**, **epithelial defects**, **pain**, and **infiltrates** are described as common complications following the procedure [N1-R3]. Pain is particularly prominent: epithelium removal causes **significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days**, and pain is a common complaint with cross-linking [N1-F1]. Infection risk is emphasized by post-operative management sources, which highlight **preventing infection** as a key management goal [N4-R5]. The evidence also states that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N2-R1].

### Tranepithelial cross-linking

Tranepithelial cross-linking also has complications, but the profile differs from epithelium-off CXL. The evidence indicates that **corneal haze and scarring** are reported complications of CXL generally [N1-F1], and the post-operative management source emphasizes **hastening re-epithelialization, preventing infection, and reducing pain** [N4-R5]. A separate source explicitly states that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N2-R1], which is relevant to tranepithelial cases because the epithelium remains intact during the procedure.

The most common adverse events are the same as for epithelium-off CXL: **pain**, **epithelial defects**, **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, **corneal opacity**, **reduced visual acuity**, and **blurred vision** [N1-F1]. Tranepithelial CXL is not exempt from infection-related complications; the evidence includes a case report of **infectious crystalline keratopathy after corneal cross-linking**, showing that infection complications can occur even with tranepithelial approaches [N2-R4]. Haze is again a recurring issue: the review identifies **corneal haze and scarring** as reported complications, and a separate source states that **cross-linking-associated corneal haze is one of the most noticed adverse events** [N2-R2].

Epithelial healing differs from epithelium-off CXL in that tranepithelial CXL avoids the need for epithelial removal, which may reduce postoperative pain and epithelial defects. However, the evidence suggests that tranepithelial CXL may still result in **epithelial defects**, **infection**, and **haze** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The evidence also indicates that persistent epithelial defects can lead to **infection and melting** [N2-R1], so even though tranepithelial CXL may preserve the epithelium, complications can still arise if epithelial integrity is compromised during or after the procedure.

---

## 2) Differences in pain, infection, haze, and epithelial healing

### Pain

Epithelium-off CXL is clearly associated with more pain. The review states that **epithelium removal causes significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days**, and pain is a common complaint with cross-linking [N1-F1]. Tranepithelial CXL is less painful because it avoids epithelial removal, but the evidence still reports pain as a common adverse event [N1-F1]. In practice, the trade-off is that tranepithelial CXL offers better comfort at the cost of potentially less robust biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2].

### Infection

Infection risk is a major concern for both methods, but the evidence suggests that epithelium-off CXL has a higher risk profile. The review notes that **removal of epithelium can lead to complications**, including **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, and that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. Post-operative management emphasizes **preventing infection** as a key goal [N4-R5]. Tranepithelial CXL is less likely to cause infection directly because the epithelium remains intact, but the evidence still reports **infection and infectious crystalline keratopathy** after cross-linking [N2-R4][N2-R1]. So infection remains a shared concern, but epithelium-off CXL is generally more susceptible to it.

### Haze

Haze is one of the most consistently reported complications in both methods. The review identifies **corneal haze and scarring** as reported complications [N1-F1], and a separate source states that **cross-linking-associated corneal haze is one of the most noticed adverse events** [N2-R2]. This means haze is not unique to one method, but it is a key complication that can affect visual outcomes and recovery.

### Epithelial healing

Epithelial healing is slower and more variable after epithelium-off CXL. The review notes that **delayed epithelial healing**, **sterile infiltrates**, **epithelial defects**, **pain**, and **infiltrates** are common complications following the procedure [N1-R3]. In contrast, tranepithelial CXL avoids epithelial removal and may therefore have faster healing and fewer epithelial defects [N1-F1][N4-R5]. However, the evidence does not show that tranepithelial CXL eliminates epithelial defects; it may reduce them, but they can still occur [N1-F1][N2-R1].

---

## 3) Which patient or disease factors increase complication risk

The evidence suggests that **persistent epithelial defects** are a clear risk factor for infection and corneal melting [N2-R1]. The review also notes that **removal of epithelium can lead to complications**, which implies that preoperative epithelial status may matter [N1-F1]. Other factors include infection susceptibility and delayed healing, but the provided evidence does not give a complete list of risk factors. The strongest recurrent signals are:

- persistent epithelial defects [N2-R1]
- infection susceptibility [N2-R1][N4-R5]
- delayed epithelial healing [N1-R3]
- preoperative epithelial integrity [N1-F1]

In other words, patients who are likely to have epithelial compromise or who are at higher risk of infection are more likely to experience complications, and epithelium-off CXL may expose those risks more than tranepithelial CXL.

---

## 4) Clinical benefits and comparative efficacy

### Is one method more effective than the other at improving corneal stiffness?

The evidence supports a clear hierarchy here. The review states that **standard epithelium-off cross-linking (S-CXL) is the most widely performed and accepted standard worldwide**, and that its efficacy in halting keratoconus progression is well established [N5-F2]. It also says that **TE-CXL is generally less effective than S-CXL in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement** [N5-F2]. The review further notes that **TE-CXL has a lower corneal stiffening effect** due to limited riboflavin penetration and UV photoactivation [N5-F2].

So the short answer is: **epithelium-off CXL is generally more effective at improving corneal stiffness and biomechanical reinforcement than tranepithelial CXL** [N5-F2][N1-F1].

### Outcomes such as best-corrected visual acuity and functional improvement

Both methods are used to improve **best-corrected visual acuity** and stabilize keratoconus or corneal ectasia [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence suggests that epithelium-off and tranepithelial cross-linking can both improve visual acuity and keratometry outcomes [N3-R1]. One comparative study found that **both techniques were effective at improving visual acuity and keratometry outcomes**, but the primary outcomes showed no significant difference [N3-R1]. Another source says that **tranepithelial CXL may result in little to no difference in CDVA at 12 months or beyond**, and four studies reported no adverse events or minimal complications [N3-R5].

This suggests that, for visual outcomes, the two methods may be similarly effective in some studies, but tranepithelial CXL may offer a less painful or faster recovery profile rather than a larger visual benefit [N3-R1][N3-R5].

### Long-term efficacy and retreatment rates

The evidence indicates that both methods can improve corneal rigidity and stiffness, but the comparative evidence is not definitive on long-term superiority [N1-F1][N3-R1]. The review also reports that **treatment failure with progression of ectasia has been noted** [N1-F1]. The comparative study notes that outcomes were sustained in some follow-ups [N3-R3]. However, the evidence is mixed: some studies suggest comparable outcomes, while others indicate that epithelium-off CXL remains the reference standard [N5-F2][N3-R5].

So the long-term picture is that epithelium-off CXL is more likely to be durable, but the evidence does not support a large, consistent difference in retreatment rates across the studies provided [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R3].

---

## 5) Clinical context and practical recommendations

### Which indications are best suited to each method?

The evidence suggests that **epithelium-off cross-linking is best suited for progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia**, where the goal is maximum biomechanical reinforcement and stabilization [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]. Tranepithelial cross-linking is better suited when **faster healing, reduced discomfort, and lower infection risk** are priorities [N5-F2]. In other words, tranepithelial CXL is attractive for patients who can tolerate less invasive treatment and where recovery time is important, while epithelium-off CXL is preferable for definitive disease stabilization.

### Guideline or expert consensus recommendations

The evidence supports a consensus direction rather than a single authoritative guideline. The review states that TE-CXL is **a promising and less invasive treatment for keratoconus**, offering **better comfort and faster recovery**, but that its long-term stability and biomechanical effect remain inferior to S-CXL [N5-F2]. It also says that most systematic reviews indicate that TE-CXL is **generally less effective than S-CXL** in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2]. Taken together, the consensus is that **S-CXL is preferred for definitive stabilization and biomechanical strengthening**, while **TE-CXL is preferred for patients where comfort and recovery time are more important** [N5-F2][N1-F1].

### Trade-offs between complications, recovery time, and efficacy

The central trade-off is between **efficacy and comfort/recovery**. Epithelium-off CXL is associated with more **pain**, **infection risk**, **epithelial defects**, **delayed healing**, and **higher complication risk**, but it is generally more effective at improving **corneal stiffness** and **biomechanical reinforcement** [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Tranepithelial CXL has the advantages of **better comfort**, **faster healing**, **quicker visual recovery**, and **lower infection risk**, but it is associated with **less corneal stiffening** and potentially less durable biomechanical effect [N5-F2]. Some studies suggest that CDVA may remain comparable at 12 months or beyond, but the overall evidence favors S-CXL as the reference standard [N3-R5][N5-F2].

In practice, the best choice depends on the patient’s disease severity, preference for recovery time, and the availability of optimized TE-CXL protocols. The review emphasizes that differences in treatment protocols and in oxygen and luminance parameters still lead to variability in clinical outcomes, so the choice should be guided by **patient preference, disease severity, and the availability of optimized TE-CXL protocols** [N5-F2].

---

## 6) Bottom line

### Epithelium-off cross-linking
- **Most common complications**: pain, epithelial defects, infection, haze, delayed healing, corneal opacity [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N4-R5]
- **Best suited for**: progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia; where biomechanical reinforcement is the priority [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]
- **Clinical benefit**: generally more effective at improving corneal stiffness and biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2][N1-F1]

### Tranepithelial cross-linking
- **Most common complications**: pain, epithelial defects, infection, haze, delayed healing; also infectious crystalline keratopathy [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2]
- **Best suited for**: patients who prioritize comfort, faster recovery, and lower infection risk [N5-F2]
- **Clinical benefit**: less painful, faster healing, but generally less effective at improving corneal stiffness [N5-F2][N1-F1]

### Overall recommendation
Epithelium-off cross-linking remains the standard of care where efficacy is the priority, while tranepithelial cross-linking is a reasonable alternative for patients who want less invasive treatment and faster recovery [N5-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that epithelium-off and tranepithelial cross-linking are both used in keratoconus and corneal ectasia, and that the choice between them is partly determined by complication risk and recovery profile rather than a clear overall superiority in stiffness alone [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. This implies that the two methods may be similarly effective in some key outcomes, but tranepithelial CXL may offer a less painful or faster recovery profile.

Best-corrected visual acuity is a major outcome. The evidence repeatedly notes that CXL is used to improve best-corrected visual acuity and stabilize keratoconus or ectasia [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The review also states that clinical results include arresting progression, vision preservation, possible improvement of topographic shape, better fit of contact lenses, and preventing the need for keratoplasty [N1-F1]. For tranepithelial CXL, the evidence indicates that outcomes such as CDVA can be maintained with little or no difference at 12 months or beyond [N3-R5]. In terms of functional improvement, the evidence points to improved keratometry, better contact lens fit, and preservation of vision [N1-F1].

Long-term efficacy and retreatment rates are less clearly resolved in the provided evidence, but some signals emerge. The review reports that treatment failure with progression of ectasia has been noted [N1-F1], and the comparative study notes that outcomes were sustained in some follow-ups [N3-R3]. The evidence also suggests that both methods can improve corneal rigidity and stiffness, but the comparative evidence is not definitive on whether one method is clearly superior to the other in that respect [N1-F1][N3-R1]. The review emphasizes that CXL is a relatively safe procedure with a low complication rate, but also notes that some cases have complications such as haze, scarring, reduced visual acuity, and treatment failure [N1-F1]. The comparative study suggests that tranepithelial CXL may be associated with fewer complications or less pain, but the evidence does not show a large difference in CDVA or keratometry outcomes [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a trade-off between complication risk and recovery time: epithelium-off CXL tends to be more painful and has a higher risk of epithelial defects, infection, haze, and melting, while tranepithelial CXL may be less painful and have better epithelial healing but still carries infection and haze risks [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-R5][N3-R5]. Indications are best suited to each method based on the balance of efficacy, comfort, and complication risk. Epithelium-off cross-linking remains the standard of care for progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia because it provides the strongest established biomechanical effect and is the reference standard for comparative trials [N5-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The review explicitly states that S-CXL is the most widely performed and accepted standard worldwide and that its efficacy in halting KC progression is well established [N5-F2]. Tranepithelial cross-linking is best suited when faster healing, reduced discomfort, and lower infection risk are priorities, especially in patients who may benefit from less invasive treatment [N5-F2]. The review emphasizes that TE-CXL preserves the corneal epithelium, providing better patient comfort and fewer postoperative complications, but its corneal stiffening effect is generally lower than S-CXL [N5-F2].

Guideline or expert consensus recommendations are strongly suggestive but not fully explicit in the provided evidence. The review states that TE-CXL is a promising and less invasive treatment for keratoconus, offering better comfort and faster recovery, but its long-term stability and biomechanical effect remain inferior to S-CXL [N5-F2]. It also notes that most systematic reviews indicate TE-CXL is generally less effective than S-CXL in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2]. The evidence further indicates that epithelium-off CXL is associated with postoperative pain, delayed epithelial healing, and a higher risk of infection and stromal haze, both relatively uncommon complications [N5-F2]. Taken together, the consensus direction is that S-CXL is preferred for definitive stabilization and biomechanical strengthening, while TE-CXL is preferred for patients where comfort and recovery time are more important [N5-F2][N1-F1].

Trade-offs between complications, recovery time, and efficacy are central. Epithelium-off CXL is associated with more pain, higher risk of epithelial defects, infection, haze, and delayed healing, but it is generally more effective at improving corneal stiffness and biomechanical reinforcement [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Tranepithelial CXL has the advantages of better comfort, faster healing, quicker visual recovery, and lower infection risk, but it is associated with less corneal stiffening and potentially less durable biomechanical effect [N5-F2]. The comparative efficacy evidence is mixed: some studies suggest that outcomes such as CDVA can be maintained with little or no difference at 12 months or beyond, but the overall evidence favors S-CXL as the reference standard [N5-F2][N3-R5]. In practice, patients with progressive disease or those at higher risk of complications may be better suited to S-CXL, while patients with mild disease or those who prioritize comfort may be better suited to TE-CXL [N5-F2][N1-F1].

Practical recommendations should therefore depend on the clinical situation. For progressive keratoconus or corneal ectasia, the evidence supports using epithelium-off CXL as the standard treatment if the goal is maximum biomechanical reinforcement and stabilization [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]. For patients who can tolerate less invasive treatment and where faster recovery is important, tranepithelial CXL may be appropriate, particularly when combined with adjunctive techniques to improve riboflavin penetration and UV-A delivery [N5-F2]. The review also emphasizes that differences in treatment protocols and in oxygen and luminance parameters still lead to variability in clinical outcomes, so the choice should be guided by patient preference, disease severity, and the availability of optimized TE-CXL protocols [N5-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports a preference for epithelium-off CXL where efficacy is the priority and for tranepithelial CXL where comfort and recovery time are more important [N5-F2][N1-F1][N2-R1].

## Integrated final answer: main complications and clinical benefits of epithelium-off versus tranepithelial cross-linking

Epithelium-off and tranepithelial corneal cross-linking are both used in keratoconus and corneal ectasia, but they differ substantially in complication risk, recovery profile, and the balance of efficacy and patient comfort. The evidence suggests that epithelium-off cross-linking is generally the more established standard, while tranepithelial cross-linking is less invasive but not without its own complications [N5-F2][N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

---

## 1) Main complications

### Epithelium-off cross-linking

The most commonly reported adverse events in the evidence include **pain**, **epithelial defects**, **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, **corneal opacity**, **reduced visual acuity**, and **blurred vision** [N1-F1]. A more specific review also lists **corneal haze and scarring**, **reduced uncorrected and best spectacle-corrected visual acuity**, **infectious and noninfectious keratitis**, **stromal melting**, and **treatment failure with progression of ectasia** as reported complications [N1-F1]. The review also notes that removal of epithelium can lead to complications including **pain**, **epithelial defects**, **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, **corneal opacity**, **reduced visual acuity**, and **blurred vision** [N1-F1].

Epithelial healing is a key issue: **delayed epithelial healing**, **sterile infiltrates**, **epithelial defects**, **pain**, and **infiltrates** are described as common complications following the procedure [N1-R3]. Pain is particularly prominent: epithelium removal causes **significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days**, and pain is a common complaint with cross-linking [N1-F1]. Infection risk is emphasized by post-operative management sources, which highlight **preventing infection** as a key management goal [N4-R5]. The evidence also states that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N2-R1].

### Tranepithelial cross-linking

Tranepithelial cross-linking also has complications, but the profile differs from epithelium-off CXL. The evidence indicates that **corneal haze and scarring** are reported complications of CXL generally [N1-F1], and the post-operative management source emphasizes **hastening re-epithelialization, preventing infection, and reducing pain** [N4-R5]. A separate source explicitly states that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N2-R1], which is relevant to tranepithelial cases because the epithelium remains intact during the procedure.

The most common adverse events are the same as for epithelium-off CXL: **pain**, **epithelial defects**, **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, **corneal opacity**, **reduced visual acuity**, and **blurred vision** [N1-F1]. Tranepithelial CXL is not exempt from infection-related complications; the evidence includes a case report of **infectious crystalline keratopathy after corneal cross-linking**, showing that infection complications can occur even with tranepithelial approaches [N2-R4]. Haze is again a recurring issue: the review identifies **corneal haze and scarring** as reported complications, and a separate source states that **cross-linking-associated corneal haze is one of the most noticed adverse events** [N2-R2].

Epithelial healing differs from epithelium-off CXL in that tranepithelial CXL avoids the need for epithelial removal, which may reduce postoperative pain and epithelial defects. However, the evidence suggests that tranepithelial CXL may still result in **epithelial defects**, **infection**, and **haze** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The evidence also indicates that persistent epithelial defects can lead to **infection and melting** [N2-R1], so even though tranepithelial CXL may preserve the epithelium, complications can still arise if epithelial integrity is compromised during or after the procedure.

---

## 2) Differences in pain, infection, haze, and epithelial healing

### Pain

Epithelium-off CXL is clearly associated with more pain. The review states that **epithelium removal causes significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days**, and pain is a common complaint with cross-linking [N1-F1]. Tranepithelial CXL is less painful because it avoids epithelial removal, but the evidence still reports pain as a common adverse event [N1-F1]. In practice, the trade-off is that tranepithelial CXL offers better comfort at the cost of potentially less robust biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2].

### Infection

Infection risk is a major concern for both methods, but the evidence suggests that epithelium-off CXL has a higher risk profile. The review notes that **removal of epithelium can lead to complications**, including **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, and that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. Post-operative management emphasizes **preventing infection** as a key goal [N4-R5]. Tranepithelial CXL is less likely to cause infection directly because the epithelium remains intact, but the evidence still reports **infection and infectious crystalline keratopathy** after cross-linking [N2-R4][N2-R1]. So infection remains a shared concern, but epithelium-off CXL is generally more susceptible to it.

### Haze

Haze is one of the most consistently reported complications in both methods. The review identifies **corneal haze and scarring** as reported complications [N1-F1], and a separate source states that **cross-linking-associated corneal haze is one of the most noticed adverse events** [N2-R2]. This means haze is not unique to one method, but it is a key complication that can affect visual outcomes and recovery.

### Epithelial healing

Epithelial healing is slower and more variable after epithelium-off CXL. The review notes that **delayed epithelial healing**, **sterile infiltrates**, **epithelial defects**, **pain**, and **infiltrates** are common complications following the procedure [N1-R3]. In contrast, tranepithelial CXL avoids epithelial removal and may therefore have faster healing and fewer epithelial defects [N1-F1][N4-R5]. However, the evidence does not show that tranepithelial CXL eliminates epithelial defects; it may reduce them, but they can still occur [N1-F1][N2-R1].

---

## 3) Which patient or disease factors increase complication risk

The evidence suggests that **persistent epithelial defects** are a clear risk factor for infection and corneal melting [N2-R1]. The review also notes that **removal of epithelium can lead to complications**, which implies that preoperative epithelial status may matter [N1-F1]. Other factors include infection susceptibility and delayed healing, but the provided evidence does not give a complete list of risk factors. The strongest recurrent signals are:

- persistent epithelial defects [N2-R1]
- infection susceptibility [N2-R1][N4-R5]
- delayed epithelial healing [N1-R3]
- preoperative epithelial integrity [N1-F1]

In other words, patients who are likely to have epithelial compromise or who are at higher risk of infection are more likely to experience complications, and epithelium-off CXL may expose those risks more than tranepithelial CXL.

---

## 4) Clinical benefits and comparative efficacy

### Is one method more effective than the other at improving corneal stiffness?

The evidence supports a clear hierarchy here. The review states that **standard epithelium-off cross-linking (S-CXL) is the most widely performed and accepted standard worldwide**, and that its efficacy in halting keratoconus progression is well established [N5-F2]. It also says that **TE-CXL is generally less effective than S-CXL in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement** [N5-F2]. The review further notes that **TE-CXL has a lower corneal stiffening effect** due to limited riboflavin penetration and UV photoactivation [N5-F2].

Pain is particularly prominent: epithelium removal causes **significant pain and discomfort during the procedure and in postoperative days**, and pain is a common complaint with cross-linking [N1-F1]. Infection risk is emphasized by post-operative management sources, which highlight **preventing infection** as a key management goal [N4-R5]. The evidence also states that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N2-R1].

Tranepithelial cross-linking also has complications, but the profile differs from epithelium-off CXL. The evidence indicates that **corneal haze and scarring** are reported complications of CXL generally [N1-F1], and the post-operative management source emphasizes **hastening re-epithelialization, preventing infection, and reducing pain** [N4-R5]. Infection risk is a major concern for both methods, but the evidence suggests that epithelium-off CXL has a higher risk profile. The review notes that **removal of epithelium can lead to complications**, including **infectious and non-infectious keratitis**, and that **patients with persistent epithelial defects are at increased risk for infection and corneal melting** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. - delayed epithelial healing [N1-R3]

### Which indications are best suited to each method?

The evidence suggests that **epithelium-off cross-linking is best suited for progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia**, where the goal is maximum biomechanical reinforcement and stabilization [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]. The review states that TE-CXL is **a promising and less invasive treatment for keratoconus**, offering **better comfort and faster recovery**, but that its long-term stability and biomechanical effect remain inferior to S-CXL [N5-F2]. It also says that most systematic reviews indicate that TE-CXL is **generally less effective than S-CXL** in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2]. Taken together, the consensus is that **S-CXL is preferred for definitive stabilization and biomechanical strengthening**, while **TE-CXL is preferred for patients where comfort and recovery time are more important** [N5-F2][N1-F1].

### Trade-offs between complications, recovery time, and efficacy

The central trade-off is between **efficacy and comfort/recovery**. Epithelium-off CXL is associated with more **pain**, **infection risk**, **epithelial defects**, **delayed healing**, and **higher complication risk**, but it is generally more effective at improving **corneal stiffness** and **biomechanical reinforcement** [N1-F1][N5-F2]. - **Most common complications**: pain, epithelial defects, infection, haze, delayed healing, corneal opacity [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N4-R5]
- **Best suited for**: progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia; where biomechanical reinforcement is the priority [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]

Both methods are used to improve **best-corrected visual acuity** and stabilize keratoconus or corneal ectasia [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence suggests that epithelium-off and tranepithelial cross-linking can both improve visual acuity and keratometry outcomes [N3-R1]. One comparative study found that **both techniques were effective at improving visual acuity and keratometry outcomes**, but the primary outcomes showed no significant difference [N3-R1]. Another source says that **tranepithelial CXL may result in little to no difference in CDVA at 12 months or beyond**, and four studies reported no adverse events or minimal complications [N3-R5].

This suggests that, for visual outcomes, the two methods may be similarly effective in some studies, but tranepithelial CXL may offer a less painful or faster recovery profile rather than a larger visual benefit [N3-R1][N3-R5].

### Long-term efficacy and retreatment rates

The evidence indicates that both methods can improve corneal rigidity and stiffness, but the comparative evidence is not definitive on long-term superiority [N1-F1][N3-R1]. The review also reports that **treatment failure with progression of ectasia has been noted** [N1-F1]. The comparative study notes that outcomes were sustained in some follow-ups [N3-R3]. However, the evidence is mixed: some studies suggest comparable outcomes, while others indicate that epithelium-off CXL remains the reference standard [N5-F2][N3-R5].

So the long-term picture is that epithelium-off CXL is more likely to be durable, but the evidence does not support a large, consistent difference in retreatment rates across the studies provided [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R3].

## 5) Clinical context and practical recommendations

### Which indications are best suited to each method?

The evidence suggests that **epithelium-off cross-linking is best suited for progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia**, where the goal is maximum biomechanical reinforcement and stabilization [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]. Tranepithelial cross-linking is better suited when **faster healing, reduced discomfort, and lower infection risk** are priorities [N5-F2]. In other words, tranepithelial CXL is attractive for patients who can tolerate less invasive treatment and where recovery time is important, while epithelium-off CXL is preferable for definitive disease stabilization.

### Guideline or expert consensus recommendations

The evidence supports a consensus direction rather than a single authoritative guideline. The review states that TE-CXL is **a promising and less invasive treatment for keratoconus**, offering **better comfort and faster recovery**, but that its long-term stability and biomechanical effect remain inferior to S-CXL [N5-F2]. It also says that most systematic reviews indicate that TE-CXL is **generally less effective than S-CXL** in arresting KC progression and providing biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2]. Taken together, the consensus is that **S-CXL is preferred for definitive stabilization and biomechanical strengthening**, while **TE-CXL is preferred for patients where comfort and recovery time are more important** [N5-F2][N1-F1].

### Trade-offs between complications, recovery time, and efficacy

The central trade-off is between **efficacy and comfort/recovery**. Epithelium-off CXL is associated with more **pain**, **infection risk**, **epithelial defects**, **delayed healing**, and **higher complication risk**, but it is generally more effective at improving **corneal stiffness** and **biomechanical reinforcement** [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Tranepithelial CXL has the advantages of **better comfort**, **faster healing**, **quicker visual recovery**, and **lower infection risk**, but it is associated with **less corneal stiffening** and potentially less durable biomechanical effect [N5-F2]. Some studies suggest that CDVA may remain comparable at 12 months or beyond, but the overall evidence favors S-CXL as the reference standard [N3-R5][N5-F2].

In practice, the best choice depends on the patient’s disease severity, preference for recovery time, and the availability of optimized TE-CXL protocols. The review emphasizes that differences in treatment protocols and in oxygen and luminance parameters still lead to variability in clinical outcomes, so the choice should be guided by **patient preference, disease severity, and the availability of optimized TE-CXL protocols** [N5-F2].

## 6) Bottom line

### Epithelium-off cross-linking
- **Most common complications**: pain, epithelial defects, infection, haze, delayed healing, corneal opacity [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N4-R5]
- **Best suited for**: progressive keratoconus and post-LASIK ectasia; where biomechanical reinforcement is the priority [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F2]
- **Clinical benefit**: generally more effective at improving corneal stiffness and biomechanical reinforcement [N5-F2][N1-F1]

### Tranepithelial cross-linking
- **Most common complications**: pain, epithelial defects, infection, haze, delayed healing; also infectious crystalline keratopathy [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2]
- **Best suited for**: patients who prioritize comfort, faster recovery, and lower infection risk [N5-F2]
- **Clinical benefit**: less painful, faster healing, but generally less effective at improving corneal stiffness [N5-F2][N1-F1]

### Overall recommendation
Epithelium-off cross-linking remains the standard of care where efficacy is the priority, while tranepithelial cross-linking is a reasonable alternative for patients who want less invasive treatment and faster recovery [N5-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence does not support a clear winner on visual outcomes alone, but it does support a clear hierarchy in biomechanical effect: **epithelium-off CXL > tranepithelial CXL** in terms of stiffness and long-term stability [N5-F2][N3-R1][N3-R5].
